t.1.9.1: Then Sumantra, urged by the king, spoke these words: "Listen to me, together with your ministers, as I tell how Ṛṣyaśṛṅga was brought here."
t.1.9.2: The family priest, together with the ministers, said this to Romapāda: "We have thought out a means, and this means is free from any danger."
t.1.9.3: Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, a dweller of the forest devoted to austerity and the study of the Veda, knew nothing of women, of the objects of the senses, or of pleasure.
t.1.9.4: With pleasing objects of the senses that agitate the minds of men, we shall bring him to the city; let this be resolved upon at once.
t.1.9.5: Let beautiful courtesans, finely adorned, go there; honored by us, they will entice him by various means and bring him here.
t.1.9.6: Having heard this, the king replied to the purohita, "So be it." Then the purohita and the ministers, they too did accordingly.
t.1.9.7: The foremost courtesans, having heard that, entered the great forest, and not far from this hermitage they strive to catch sight of him.
t.1.9.8: Ever content, he never once strayed beyond the hermitage of his father, the stern son of a sage, who always dwelt in that hermitage.
t.1.9.9: From his very birth that ascetic had never before seen a woman or a man, or any other creature born of city or kingdom.
t.1.9.10: Then one day the son of Vibhāṇḍaka came by chance to that place, and there he saw those beautiful women.
t.1.9.11: Those young women in colorful attire, singing in sweet voices, all approached the sage's son and spoke these words.
t.1.9.12: Who are you, O brahmin, and what are you doing? We wish to know. You wander alone in this dreadful, desolate forest; tell us.
t.1.9.13: Those women in the forest, of desirable form, were such as had never before been seen by him; out of affection, the thought arose in him to tell his own father about them.
t.1.9.14: Our father is Vibhāṇḍaka, and I am his own son, born of his body. Ṛṣyaśṛṅga is my name, and my name and my deeds are renowned on earth.
t.1.9.15: Here, near us, is our hermitage, O you of lovely appearance; there I shall duly offer worship to all of you according to the prescribed rite.
t.1.9.16: Hearing the words of the sage's son, all of them resolved to see that hermitage, and they all went there with him.
t.1.9.17: Then the sage's son honored the women who had come, saying, "Here is water to receive you, here is water for your feet, and here are our roots and fruits."
t.1.9.18: Having accepted that worship, all of them, though eager, were afraid of the sage, and quickly set their minds on departing.
t.1.9.19: These are our choicest fruits too, O twice-born one; accept them, may good fortune be yours, and eat them without delay.
t.1.9.20: Then all those women, filled with delight, embraced him and gave him modakas and many other fine and varied delicacies.
t.1.9.21: Having tasted them, the radiant one took them for fruits, such as had never before been tasted by those who dwell always in the forest.
t.1.9.22: Then, taking leave of the brahmin and telling him of a vow they had to observe, those women, afraid of his father, went away on that pretext.
t.1.9.23: When all those women had gone, the twice-born son of Kāśyapa grew troubled at heart, and sorrow kept churning within him.
t.1.9.24: Then, on the next day, that mighty one came to the place where he had seen those charming, finely adorned chief courtesans.
t.1.9.25: And as soon as they saw the brahmin approaching, they were glad at heart; then all of them drew near and spoke these words to him.
t.1.9.26: "Come, gentle one, to our hermitage," they said, "there too this splendid rite of welcome shall be performed for you, and all the more fully."
t.1.9.28: And as that great-souled brahmin was being brought there, the god suddenly poured down rain, gladdening the world at that time.
t.1.9.27: Having heard the heart-captivating words of all those women, he made up his mind to go, and then the women led him away.
t.1.9.29: When the brahmin arrived in his own realm, accompanied by the rain itself, the king went out to meet the sage and, bowing humbly, touched the ground with his head.
t.1.9.31: Having entered the inner apartments, that king, with a tranquil mind, gave his daughter Śāntā to him in marriage according to the prescribed rites, and he attained joy.
t.1.9.30: With a well-collected mind he duly offered him the guest-water, and he asked the foremost of the brahmins for their favour, so that anger might not take hold of the brahmin.
t.1.9.32: Thus the greatly radiant Ṛṣyaśṛṅga dwelt there with his wife Śāntā, well honored with every object of desire.
